title: Succinylcholine — Pediatric RSI Paralysis
sources: FDA boxed warning — succinylcholine chloride prescribing information (hyperkalemic cardiac arrest in children with undiagnosed skeletal-muscle myopathy).

changelog.change: Initial entry — the depolarizing-paralytic sibling named in peds-rocuronium-rsi's buildNote as the still-needed complement of that set.

purpose: Fastest-onset paralytic for RSI when a depolarizing agent is appropriate — the alternative to rocuronium when the fastest possible paralysis and the shortest duration both matter.

doses.notes: Infants and young children often need the higher end of the range (larger volume of distribution). Onset ~30-60 s, duration 5-10 min — the fastest-recovering paralytic available.
Slower onset (~2-3 min) than IV/IO — use only when vascular access genuinely isn't available.

contraindications: Hyperkalemia risk: renal failure, burns > 24 h old, denervation injury or prolonged immobilization, myopathies — depolarization can trigger a dangerous potassium efflux
Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia
Known or suspected pseudocholinesterase deficiency (prolonged paralysis)

Undiagnosed skeletal-muscle myopathy (e.g. Duchenne muscular dystrophy) — FDA boxed warning: succinylcholine has caused acute rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest in young boys with unrecognized myopathy, most often after a first anesthetic exposure. Favor rocuronium when a myopathy can't be confidently excluded (non-emergent walking child with unexplained weakness/delayed milestones, or any elective use in a young boy without a clear diagnosis).
reversal: None — recovery is by spontaneous pseudocholinesterase hydrolysis, not a reversal agent. This is exactly why it's chosen when a short duration matters more than reversibility.
buildNote: Depolarizing-agent sibling of peds-rocuronium-rsi (the non-depolarizing default when succinylcholine is contraindicated). Cross-linked both directions.
